aldemar.headline: The Fed held with two dissents for a hike — and Alphabet missed while this book held nothing
aldemar.standfirst: The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on a 10-2 vote, with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a hike; the statement called growth strong and inflation elevated, and the ten-year rose 5.2bp to 5.044% while the two-year barely moved. Stocks edged up — S&P +0.28%, a third straight gain — and WTI rose 2.9% to $102.78 on a claimed strike on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery. After the close Alphabet missed on revenue and earnings for the first time in nearly four years — EPS $2.12 against about $3.02, free cash flow minus $9.07bn despite Cloud growth of 103% — and fell about 9% after hours, while Microsoft rose about 2.6% on Azure growth of 48%. The book has no open positions: PLTR was closed on 15 October at 194.25, about +1R. Q4 is +45.38 realised across four exits, heat 0R.

The regular session was calm; the news came after it. Crude +2.88% at 1.39σ was the only reading above one sigma. Every other instrument rose by less than half a percent: the S&P +0.28% at 0.45σ, the Russell +0.41% at 0.45σ, the Dow +0.19% at 0.35σ, the Nasdaq +0.27% at 0.24σ and gold +0.19% at 0.20σ. The indices, precisely. The S&P rose 21.38 points to 7,743.98, a third straight gain; the Nasdaq 72.04 to 26,549.85; the Dow 97.53 to 52,475.10; the Russell 11.64 to 2,830.51. The semiconductor index rose 1.75% to 11,684, with SK Hynix up 13.3%, Oracle 10.7% and Vertiv 16.5%, while Nvidia fell 1.17%. Week to date: Nasdaq +2.3%, Russell +2.0%, S&P +1.6%, Dow +0.5%. For the year: Nasdaq +14.2%, Russell +14.0%, S&P +13.1%, Dow +9.2%.

The bond market answered the Fed by steepening. The two-year jumped right after the statement and then fell back as traders trimmed hike bets, closing at 4.731%, little changed. The long end did not come back: ten-year +5.2bp to 5.044%, thirty-year +5.6bp to 5.360%. A front end that is calm and a long end that sells off is the market saying the Fed is not in a hurry and that it does not trust inflation to fall on its own. Prediction markets moved the December hike to about 82%, from 77% before the decision; Kalshi had about 81%.

After the close, a split that matters for every AI name. Alphabet's Class A shares fell about 10% on the double miss. Microsoft rose about 2.6% on revenue of $92.28bn and Azure growth of 48%. ServiceNow fell about 18% and Fortinet about 26%. Two hyperscalers both spending heavily drew opposite verdicts; the difference was a clean beat and the cash line, not the decision to spend.

Commodities. WTI settled $102.78, up 2.88%, and Brent $115.32, up $1.44. Spot gold rose 0.19% to $4,067.78. The dollar index slipped 0.16% to 102.16.

There are no holdings to cover. Of the names this book exited this month, two report inside the next week: Amazon on Thursday and Palantir on 2 November. Palantir has guided Q3 revenue to $2.160-2.164bn, and Rosenblatt raised its target to $260 on Tuesday. They are worth watching as information about the AI trade, and as possible re-entries, but neither is exposure.

Microsoft beat and rose, Alphabet missed and fell — and cash was the difference

1. Alphabet's problem was not the one Pichai flagged. On 21 October he said Google Cloud was giving up short-term revenue to feed DeepMind. Cloud then grew 103% to $30.71bn with operating income of $11.12bn. What missed was earnings — $2.12 against about $3.02, hit by an $8.66bn equity-securities loss — and cash: capex of $51.36bn, operating cash flow down to $42.29bn, and free cash flow of minus $9.07bn, worse than the minus $2.27bn expected. Last week the market marked Meta down 7% for negative free cash flow and then forgave it when Meta named a funding source. Alphabet has not named one.

2. Microsoft drew the opposite verdict on the same evening. Revenue of $92.28bn beat, Azure grew 48%, and the shares rose about 2.6% after hours. Both companies are spending heavily on AI capacity; one delivered a clean beat and one did not. Elsewhere after hours ServiceNow fell about 18% and Fortinet about 26% — two large software names marked down hard in one night. Amazon reports on Thursday, so the third hyperscaler is judged within 24 hours.

3. The Fed held, two members wanted to hike, and the long end sold. The 10-2 vote with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a hike, a statement calling growth strong and inflation elevated, and no mention of energy add up to a committee leaning toward tightening without committing. Warsh declined to prejudge December. The front end barely moved; the ten-year rose 5.2 basis points to 5.044% and the thirty-year 5.6. September PCE on Thursday is the next input, and crude went back above $100 the same afternoon.

A claimed strike on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery puts crude back above $100

The Houthis claimed a missile strike on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, a plant with 550,000 barrels a day of capacity. Saudi authorities had not confirmed it. Yemeni government forces separately reported a Houthi attack on Aden airport. Traders also priced the reported US and Israeli plans for strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms. WTI settled $102.78, up $2.88, and Brent $115.32, up $1.44. WTI recovered most of Monday's and Tuesday's fall; Brent about half of it.

The inventory data pointed the same way. US crude stocks fell 1.9m barrels in the week to 23 October, against an expected build of about 15,000. With the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest level since 1982, there is little domestic cushion if a refinery claim turns out to be true.

The diplomacy has still produced nothing on the record. Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials went to Tehran on Monday and Qatari mediators on Sunday; Iran has said there will be no talks with Washington until its demands are met. Crude fell two days on the meetings and rose one on the attacks. For this book the channel is the same as all month: crude feeds Thursday's PCE, PCE feeds the long end, and the long end sold off on Wednesday before PCE arrived.

weekly.headline: Three exits, heat halved, and a board that printed two-sigma days in opposite directions
weekly.standfirst: The week's most unusual move was gold, down 4.14% — the only two-sigma reading on the board — while crude rose 5.97% to $103.27 and Brent reached its highest close since late April at $116.72. The Russell gained 2.0% and the Dow 0.4%, while the S&P lost 0.5% in a second consecutive weekly loss and the Nasdaq 0.7%. Four sessions, four tape shapes, ending with two-sigma days in opposite halves of the market: Nasdaq −2.60% on Thursday when a filing showed Meta's forward compute commitments far above July's level and the stock fell 6.98%, then Dow −1.23% on Friday when the same cash-flow test sank Bloom Energy 11.24% on record revenue. The long end fell nine basis points across the week to 5.00% via a seventeen-point single-day collapse; France's ten-year crossed 5% for the first time since 2002, passed the US ten-year for the first time since 2013, and then Moody's held the rating at Aa3 negative. In the book AAPL was taken on Monday at 341.23 for +0.96R, the third exit of October, and PLTR rose 5.76% across the week to +0.62R. The week +8.49; Q4 +47.88 with +35.58 realised. Heat fell from 2.00R to 1.00R, leaving 2.00R spare for the first time since September.

Gold had the week, and it had it in the wrong direction for the story everything else was telling. Gold fell 4.14% at 2.23σ — the only two-sigma reading on the board — in a week when crude rose 5.97% to $103.27 and Brent reached its highest close since late April. An inflation hedge losing four percent while the oil price gains six is a market that has decided the energy shock is a demand problem rather than a price one. Behind gold: the Russell +2.00% at 1.33σ, the best index of the week, then crude at 0.97σ — a six percent week that is not unusual for this instrument, which is the measure of how violent its autumn has been — the S&P −0.47% at 0.44σ, the Dow +0.41% at 0.41σ and the Nasdaq −0.71% at 0.34σ.

The indices, precisely. The Russell 2000 rose 54.53 points, or 2.0%, to 2,775.90 and the Dow 212.75, or 0.4%, to 52,215.16, while the S&P fell 35.76, or 0.5%, to 7,623.68 — a second consecutive weekly loss — and the Nasdaq 184.69, or 0.7%, to 25,955.34. Small caps and blue chips up, technology down: that is a rotation week in aggregate, and it conceals four sessions that each looked completely different from the one before. For the year the board now reads Russell +11.8%, Nasdaq +11.7%, S&P +11.4%, Dow +8.6%.

Four sessions, four distinct tape shapes — that is the week's real finding. Monday: the Dow +1.02% and the Russell +1.65% both near 1.75σ while the Nasdaq printed two hundredths of a sigma, a rotation into value so clean it barely moved the index. Tuesday: nothing above a sigma. Wednesday: the Dow, the Nasdaq and the S&P all above one sigma together in a broad rally, with the Russell left behind. Thursday: the Nasdaq −2.60% at 2.43σ, its largest move in thirty sessions, with the Dow at 0.04σ. Friday: the Dow −1.23% at 2.01σ, its largest in thirty sessions, with the Nasdaq at 0.20σ. Two two-sigma days in a row, in opposite halves of the market. A board that does that is not expressing a view; it is relocating money.

The bond market is where the week's argument actually happened. It opened with French protests pushing US yields up four basis points on no American data and closed with the ten-year at 5.00%, nine basis points below the 5.09% it started from. In between: Tuesday's thirty-year fell 6bp on September housing starts, which came in at a 1.221m annual pace against 1.305m expected with single-family permits at a three-and-a-half-year low; Wednesday the long end did not move at all while France's ten-year crossed 5% for the first time since 2002; and Thursday the ten-year fell about seventeen basis points to 4.96%, its largest one-day drop since August 2025, on the AI de-rating. Friday gave four of those back. A hold at 3.75-4.00% is now 90.6% priced for Wednesday.

And France went from a story to a non-event inside five sessions. The ten-year OAT ended the week at a 24-year high, having crossed 5% on Wednesday for the first time since 2002 and passed the American ten-year on Thursday for the first time since the 2013 euro-area crisis. Carrefour fell nearly 14% on riot damage, more than 2,400 arrests were recorded, several cities imposed curfews. Then on Friday Moody's held the rating at Aa3 with a negative outlook — no downgrade — and French yields eased. Across all five sessions the honest conclusion is the one this brief reached on Tuesday and then kept re-testing: French fiscal stress is not setting the price of American debt.

AAPL banked at +1R, and heat finally fell

The week's defining event is not a price. It is that heat fell from 2.00R to 1.00R. AAPL was taken on Monday the 19th at 341.23 for +19.27 and +0.96R against its 19.97 of initial risk — the third exit of October, after AMZN on the 15th and OKTA on the 16th. That leaves one position and 2.00R of unused capacity against a 3.0R cap. For the whole of September and most of October this book could not act in either direction. It can now, and the week it gained that freedom is the week the complex it would have bought into printed a two-sigma collapse. The timing is worth sitting with rather than acting on.

PLTR had the better week of the two books, and it earned it late. From the 16th's close of 186.03 it rose to 196.75, +5.76% and +10.72 on one share, taking the position from +0.08R to +0.62R. The path was not smooth: the week's low of 186.16 came on Monday, 1.71 above the 184.45 entry, then it ran to 201.72 by Wednesday on the Knox FedRAMP authorisation and the software rally, gave back 2.74% on Thursday and finished green on a Friday when nearly three of every four S&P shares fell. It sits 11.66% above the 164.45 stop on the week's low, and reports on 2 November.

The exit is worth examining because the market made it look wrong twice and then right. AAPL went out on Monday at 341.23, against a week-start close of 343.46 — so measured on the week alone the sale gave up -2.23. Two days later Apple closed at a record 343.99, which made it look worse. In between, on the 20th, Loop Capital downgraded the stock to Hold and cut its target to $330 from $370, expecting Apple to permanently lose about 13 million iPhones from second-half plans. By Friday — launch day for the foldable, with overnight queues and limited walk-in stock — it closed at 347.73, 0.14% lower after touching a 52-week high. The honest verdict on a +0.96R exit taken on a rule rather than a view is that it cost a little and settled a lot: it is the reason heat is 1.00R going into a Fed meeting.

The quarter is +47.88, of which +35.58 is realised. That is the sentence this book could not write at any point in Q3 or in the first half of October: the banked line is now larger than the open one, so the quarter's result no longer depends on a single position. Q3 finished at +17.04, +0.84R, against the S&P's +2.0%, so Q4 is already 2.8 times Q3 with five sessions left — and the difference is not that the holdings were better. Three of them were sold while they were still worth selling. The week itself was +8.49, all of it PLTR. On $184.45 of committed capital the one open position is +6.67% since entry.

The AI trade was re-priced on cash flow, not on growth

1. The week's one durable idea: the market stopped asking what the money is for and started asking where it comes from. On Wednesday Meta reported revenue up 26% to $64.60bn, raised the floor of its 2026 capital-expenditure range to $135bn and rose about 3% after hours. On Thursday a filing showed its forward commitments — mostly computing power and data-centre leases — far above July's level, and the shares fell 6.98% to $648.85. Nothing in the results had changed; the market had simply read the balance sheet instead of the income statement and noticed that $34.9bn of quarterly capex against $32.79bn of operating cash flow is negative $2.12bn of free cash flow. On Friday the same test was applied to a company with nothing to do with AI infrastructure: Bloom Energy fell 11.24%, the worst performer in the S&P, on record revenue, because the cash flow behind it was negative.

2. Which makes Wednesday the 28th the most consequential date this book has faced. The distinction the market drew on Thursday was specific: Meta funds its data centres out of advertising, while Alphabet and Microsoft also rent capacity to outside customers, so their spending is supposed to return as cloud revenue. Except that on the 21st Sundar Pichai said Google Cloud is forgoing short-term revenue to make compute trade-offs for frontier AI, called DeepMind's capacity non-negotiable and said taking new customers who need capacity next year would be incredibly difficult. He put no number on it. Alphabet reports $195-205bn of capex and a consensus near $3.00 a share on Wednesday afternoon, the same hour the Fed decides. Alphabet fell in four of the week's five sessions, including both days the Nasdaq rose.

3. The energy shock changed character twice and ended where it started. On Tuesday September housing starts fell 5.2% to a 1.221m pace against 1.305m expected, with single-family permits at a three-and-a-half-year low and the thirty-year mortgage at 7.40% — and the long end fell six basis points, pricing the oil shock as demand destruction rather than inflation. On Thursday crude rose 2.4% while the ten-year fell seventeen basis points, which said the same thing louder. Then on Friday crude rose 3.8% and the ten-year rose four, which said the opposite. September PCE on Thursday the 29th is where that argument gets an answer, and the two readings point the long end in opposite directions.

Flows recovered, products did not, and the strikes acquired a date

The week's crude move was 5.97%, and it came in two halves. The first was diplomatic relief: on Tuesday Iran's president received Pakistan's army chief in Tehran on a new mediation proposal and crude reversed three dollars off a five-month high, and on Wednesday Russia agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, possibly as early as November — read as the first credible route to easing the global diesel shortage. Then the second half: by Thursday Iran had hardened, with president Pezeshkian saying Washington cannot expect dialogue under blockade, and by Friday Brent settled $116.72, its highest close since late April, and WTI $103.27.

The physical picture improved on crude and deteriorated on product, which is the distinction that matters for inflation. Kpler put Hormuz crude flows at about 10.3m barrels a day, 76% of pre-war, with US energy secretary Chris Wright putting Gulf flows near 80% — a chokepoint running at four-fifths of capacity while being actively mined. But refined products are down to 11% of cargoes from more than 20% before the conflict, and Middle East refinery throughput was 7.3m barrels a day in August against 9.9m in February. Crude re-routes; a cracking margin does not. That reaches the consumer through diesel, freight and airfares rather than at the pump — slower, stickier, and harder to dismiss as a shock that passes.

And the war acquired a date. On Thursday the New York Times reported that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms — energy sites, nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenals. Trump said the US is not negotiating, then accused Iran of making up fake hits on ships to drive oil higher before the vote, then said on Friday that Washington could end the war quickly. Those three statements do not reconcile. Meanwhile an attack on King Fahd International Airport at Dammam killed one person and injured eight, the IRGC Navy said four oil-carrying vessels were hit in the northern Persian Gulf and three more struck mines west of Hormuz, Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters, and Kpler counted at least 18 vessels attacked in a fortnight. October is the worst month for shipping attacks in and around the Strait on Washington Institute data.

The number to carry into next week is the one with no price attached. The Department of Energy authorised an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels from a Strategic Petroleum Reserve now at its lowest level since 1982, to patch a disruption at a single Louisiana refinery. Baker Hughes counted 603 oil and gas rigs, unchanged for a second week — a drilling industry declining to respond to a hundred-dollar barrel. Exxon Mobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips all closed Friday at all-time highs. The cap on the oil price has been spent and the supply response has not arrived, which is why gold falling 4.14% in the same week is the genuinely strange reading on this page.

Wednesday afternoon is the whole week. A hold at 3.75-4.00% is 90.6% priced with 9.4% on a hike, and December is where the increase sits — about 86% on the CME tool, with Goldman Sachs expecting one more quarter-point to a 4.00-4.25% peak. In the same hour Alphabet reports $195-205bn of capex against a consensus near $3.00 a share. The market has spent two sessions establishing that forward spending commitments are a liability and that negative free cash flow gets punished on record revenue; Alphabet's defence against that test is cloud revenue, and its own chief executive said six days ago that the cloud line is being held back on purpose.

Thursday is the harder one to handicap. September PCE is the measure the Fed actually targets, and it arrives with crude at a six-month high in a month where gasoline did more than half of the CPI increase. The week just gone priced the oil shock as demand destruction on Tuesday and Thursday and as inflation on Friday, and PCE will pick one. Amazon reports the same day, putting the second set of hyperscaler capital spending in front of the same jury that marked Meta down 7%.

Where this book stands going in. One position, PLTR at +0.62R and 11.66% above its 164.45 stop on the week's low, reporting on 2 November. Heat 1.00R against 3.0R with 2.00R spare, Q4 at +47.88 with +35.58 banked. The stop has not moved since September and there is no case for touching it before Wednesday; the spare capacity is an option with no expiry, and the week that created it is a poor week to spend it. The one thing to decide in advance is what the 164.45 line means if Thursday's PCE turns the long end — because a software multiple two years out is the most rate-sensitive thing in this book. Everything else in the quarter is already banked.

Gold had the week, and it had it in the wrong direction for the story everything else was telling. Gold fell 4.14% at 2.23σ — the only two-sigma reading on the board — in a week when crude rose 5.97% to $103.27 and Brent reached its highest close since late April. An inflation hedge losing four percent while the oil price gains six is a market that has decided the energy shock is a demand problem rather than a price one. Behind gold: the Russell +2.00% at 1.33σ, the best index of the week, then crude at 0.97σ — a six percent week that is not unusual for this instrument, which is the measure of how violent its autumn has been — the S&P −0.47% at 0.44σ, the Dow +0.41% at 0.41σ and the Nasdaq −0.71% at 0.34σ.

The indices, precisely. The Russell 2000 rose 54.53 points, or 2.0%, to 2,775.90 and the Dow 212.75, or 0.4%, to 52,215.16, while the S&P fell 35.76, or 0.5%, to 7,623.68 — a second consecutive weekly loss — and the Nasdaq 184.69, or 0.7%, to 25,955.34. Small caps and blue chips up, technology down: that is a rotation week in aggregate, and it conceals four sessions that each looked completely different from the one before. For the year the board now reads Russell +11.8%, Nasdaq +11.7%, S&P +11.4%, Dow +8.6%.

Four sessions, four distinct tape shapes — that is the week's real finding. Monday: the Dow +1.02% and the Russell +1.65% both near 1.75σ while the Nasdaq printed two hundredths of a sigma, a rotation into value so clean it barely moved the index. Tuesday: nothing above a sigma. Wednesday: the Dow, the Nasdaq and the S&P all above one sigma together in a broad rally, with the Russell left behind. Thursday: the Nasdaq −2.60% at 2.43σ, its largest move in thirty sessions, with the Dow at 0.04σ. Friday: the Dow −1.23% at 2.01σ, its largest in thirty sessions, with the Nasdaq at 0.20σ. Two two-sigma days in a row, in opposite halves of the market. A board that does that is not expressing a view; it is relocating money.

The bond market is where the week's argument actually happened. It opened with French protests pushing US yields up four basis points on no American data and closed with the ten-year at 5.00%, nine basis points below the 5.09% it started from. In between: Tuesday's thirty-year fell 6bp on September housing starts, which came in at a 1.221m annual pace against 1.305m expected with single-family permits at a three-and-a-half-year low; Wednesday the long end did not move at all while France's ten-year crossed 5% for the first time since 2002; and Thursday the ten-year fell about seventeen basis points to 4.96%, its largest one-day drop since August 2025, on the AI de-rating. Friday gave four of those back. A hold at 3.75-4.00% is now 90.6% priced for Wednesday.

And France went from a story to a non-event inside five sessions. The ten-year OAT ended the week at a 24-year high, having crossed 5% on Wednesday for the first time since 2002 and passed the American ten-year on Thursday for the first time since the 2013 euro-area crisis. Carrefour fell nearly 14% on riot damage, more than 2,400 arrests were recorded, several cities imposed curfews. Then on Friday Moody's held the rating at Aa3 with a negative outlook — no downgrade — and French yields eased. Across all five sessions the honest conclusion is the one this brief reached on Tuesday and then kept re-testing: French fiscal stress is not setting the price of American debt.

AAPL banked at +1R, and heat finally fell

GOOGInternet content · entered 2026-07-27 at 325.86 · stop 305.67 · 3.66% away · managed · week low 316.99-0.42R-5.83%-19.63
AAPLConsumer electronics · entered 2026-08-28 at 321.97 · exited 2026-10-19 at 341.23 · taken at +0.93R+0.93R-0.65%-2.23

The week's defining event is not a price. It is that heat fell from 2.04R to 1.01R. AAPL was taken on Monday the 19th at 341.23 for +19.26 and +0.93R against its 20.71 of initial risk — the third exit of October, after AMZN on the 15th and OKTA on the 16th. That leaves one position and 1.99R of unused capacity against a 3.0R cap. For the whole of September and most of October this book could not act in either direction. It can now, and the week it gained that freedom is the week the complex it would have bought into printed a two-sigma collapse. The timing is worth sitting with rather than acting on.

GOOG had a bad week and the shape of it is worse than the number. From the 16th's close of 336.91 it fell to 317.28, -5.83% and -19.63 on one share, taking the position from +0.55R to -0.42R — from profit to loss. It fell on four consecutive sessions after Monday, including the two days the Nasdaq rose, and the week's low of 316.99 came in the final session twenty-nine cents from the close. It now sits 3.57% above the 305.67 stop on that low. Three things caused it: a KeyCorp target cut to $410 on the 20th, Pichai saying on the 21st that Google Cloud is forgoing short-term revenue to feed frontier AI with new capacity customers incredibly difficult, and Thursday's judgement on Meta that forward spending commitments are a liability.

The exit is worth examining because the market made it look wrong twice and then right. AAPL went out on Monday at 341.23, against a week-start close of 343.46 — so measured on the week alone the sale gave up -2.23. Two days later Apple closed at a record 343.99, which made it look worse. In between, on the 20th, Loop Capital downgraded the stock to Hold and cut its target to $330 from $370, expecting Apple to permanently lose about 13 million iPhones from second-half plans. By Friday — launch day for the foldable, with overnight queues and limited walk-in stock — it closed at 347.73, 0.14% lower after touching a 52-week high. The honest verdict on a +0.93R exit taken on a rule rather than a view is that it cost a little and settled a lot: it is the reason heat is 1.01R going into a Fed meeting.

Q4 · seventeen sessions in

This week19–23 October, one exit and one holding-21.86
Q4 realisedthree closed this month, banked+34.64
Q4 netseventeen sessions into the quarter+26.06

The quarter is +26.06, of which +34.64 is realised. That is the sentence this book could not write at any point in Q3 or in the first half of October: the banked line is now larger than the open one, so the quarter's result no longer depends on a single position. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R, against the S&P's +2.0%, so Q4 is already 2.1 times Q3 with five sessions left — and the difference is not that the holdings were better. Three of them were sold while they were still worth selling. The week itself was -21.86, all of it GOOG. On $325.86 of committed capital the one open position is -2.63% since entry.

The AI trade was re-priced on cash flow, not on growth

1. The week's one durable idea: the market stopped asking what the money is for and started asking where it comes from. On Wednesday Meta reported revenue up 26% to $64.60bn, raised the floor of its 2026 capital-expenditure range to $135bn and rose about 3% after hours. On Thursday a filing showed its forward commitments — mostly computing power and data-centre leases — far above July's level, and the shares fell 6.98% to $648.85. Nothing in the results had changed; the market had simply read the balance sheet instead of the income statement and noticed that $34.9bn of quarterly capex against $32.79bn of operating cash flow is negative $2.12bn of free cash flow. On Friday the same test was applied to a company with nothing to do with AI infrastructure: Bloom Energy fell 11.24%, the worst performer in the S&P, on record revenue, because the cash flow behind it was negative.

2. Which makes Wednesday the 28th the most consequential date this book has faced. The distinction the market drew on Thursday was specific: Meta funds its data centres out of advertising, while Alphabet and Microsoft also rent capacity to outside customers, so their spending is supposed to return as cloud revenue. Except that on the 21st Sundar Pichai said Google Cloud is forgoing short-term revenue to make compute trade-offs for frontier AI, called DeepMind's capacity non-negotiable and said taking new customers who need capacity next year would be incredibly difficult. He put no number on it. Alphabet reports $195-205bn of capex and a consensus near $3.00 a share on Wednesday afternoon, the same hour the Fed decides. Alphabet fell in four of the week's five sessions, including both days the Nasdaq rose.

3. The energy shock changed character twice and ended where it started. On Tuesday September housing starts fell 5.2% to a 1.221m pace against 1.305m expected, with single-family permits at a three-and-a-half-year low and the thirty-year mortgage at 7.40% — and the long end fell six basis points, pricing the oil shock as demand destruction rather than inflation. On Thursday crude rose 2.4% while the ten-year fell seventeen basis points, which said the same thing louder. Then on Friday crude rose 3.8% and the ten-year rose four, which said the opposite. September PCE on Thursday the 29th is where that argument gets an answer, and the two readings point the long end in opposite directions.

Flows recovered, products did not, and the strikes acquired a date

The week's crude move was 5.97%, and it came in two halves. The first was diplomatic relief: on Tuesday Iran's president received Pakistan's army chief in Tehran on a new mediation proposal and crude reversed three dollars off a five-month high, and on Wednesday Russia agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, possibly as early as November — read as the first credible route to easing the global diesel shortage. Then the second half: by Thursday Iran had hardened, with president Pezeshkian saying Washington cannot expect dialogue under blockade, and by Friday Brent settled $116.72, its highest close since late April, and WTI $103.27.

The physical picture improved on crude and deteriorated on product, which is the distinction that matters for inflation. Kpler put Hormuz crude flows at about 10.3m barrels a day, 76% of pre-war, with US energy secretary Chris Wright putting Gulf flows near 80% — a chokepoint running at four-fifths of capacity while being actively mined. But refined products are down to 11% of cargoes from more than 20% before the conflict, and Middle East refinery throughput was 7.3m barrels a day in August against 9.9m in February. Crude re-routes; a cracking margin does not. That reaches the consumer through diesel, freight and airfares rather than at the pump — slower, stickier, and harder to dismiss as a shock that passes.

And the war acquired a date. On Thursday the New York Times reported that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms — energy sites, nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenals. Trump said the US is not negotiating, then accused Iran of making up fake hits on ships to drive oil higher before the vote, then said on Friday that Washington could end the war quickly. Those three statements do not reconcile. Meanwhile an attack on King Fahd International Airport at Dammam killed one person and injured eight, the IRGC Navy said four oil-carrying vessels were hit in the northern Persian Gulf and three more struck mines west of Hormuz, Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters, and Kpler counted at least 18 vessels attacked in a fortnight. October is the worst month for shipping attacks in and around the Strait on Washington Institute data.

The number to carry into next week is the one with no price attached. The Department of Energy authorised an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels from a Strategic Petroleum Reserve now at its lowest level since 1982, to patch a disruption at a single Louisiana refinery. Baker Hughes counted 603 oil and gas rigs, unchanged for a second week — a drilling industry declining to respond to a hundred-dollar barrel. Exxon Mobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips all closed Friday at all-time highs. The cap on the oil price has been spent and the supply response has not arrived, which is why gold falling 4.14% in the same week is the genuinely strange reading on this page.

Three dated events, and the first one decides the quarter

FOMC · GOOGFed decision and Alphabet Q3 on the same afternoon — a hold at 3.75-4.00% is 90.6% priced; Alphabet brings $195-205bn of capex and a $3.00 consensus to a market now pricing cash flowWed2026-10-28
PCE · AMZNSeptember PCE and Amazon Q3 — the inflation measure the Fed targets, with crude at a six-month high, and the second hyperscaler to defend its spendingThu2026-10-29
AAPLiPhone Duo in 28 more countries — the second wave after launch-day queues and limited walk-in stockFri2026-10-30
EARNINGSApple Q4 and Palantir Q3 — both out of this book now, read for the consumer and the software cycle rather than for exposureMon2026-11-02
VOTEUS midterms — the date the reported Iran strike plans sit behind, and the deadline the fuel-price politics is working toTue2026-11-03

Wednesday afternoon is the whole week. A hold at 3.75-4.00% is 90.6% priced with 9.4% on a hike, and December is where the increase sits — about 86% on the CME tool, with Goldman Sachs expecting one more quarter-point to a 4.00-4.25% peak. In the same hour Alphabet reports $195-205bn of capex against a consensus near $3.00 a share. The market has spent two sessions establishing that forward spending commitments are a liability and that negative free cash flow gets punished on record revenue; Alphabet's defence against that test is cloud revenue, and its own chief executive said six days ago that the cloud line is being held back on purpose.

Thursday is the harder one to handicap. September PCE is the measure the Fed actually targets, and it arrives with crude at a six-month high in a month where gasoline did more than half of the CPI increase. The week just gone priced the oil shock as demand destruction on Tuesday and Thursday and as inflation on Friday, and PCE will pick one. Amazon reports the same day, putting the second set of hyperscaler capital spending in front of the same jury that marked Meta down 7%.

Where this book stands going in. One position, GOOG at -0.42R and 3.57% above its 305.67 stop on the week's low, reporting Wednesday. Heat 1.01R against 3.0R with 1.99R spare, Q4 at +26.06 with +34.64 banked. The stop has not moved since September and there is no case for touching it before Wednesday; the spare capacity is an option with no expiry, and the week that created it is a poor week to spend it. The one thing to decide in advance is what the 305.67 line means on Wednesday evening if the print goes badly — because it is 11.32 a share away and it is the entire plan. Everything else in the quarter is already banked.
